newsitem.title: CHINA: China playwright seeks probe into 1989 crackdown.
newsitem.headline: China playwright seeks probe into 1989 crackdown.

text.p: One of China's leading playwrights said on Friday he had called for an investigation to clear the name of late leader Deng Xiaoping of any wrongdoing in the 1989 crackdown on student democracy demonstrations.
Deng, who died on February 19 aged 92, is widely believed to have ordered the army to crush the demonstrations on June 3-4, 1989, resulting in heavy loss of life.
He was the only political leader who could claim total control over the army as well as the party and state.
But the outspoken playwright Wu Zuguang, 79, said he believed Deng was not necessarily to blame.
"Every time people talk about the incident, Deng Xiaoping's name is mentioned. It's unfair to Deng Xiaoping," Wu said in a telephone interview.
Wu, who is also a member of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, brought up his call for a probe during group meetings of the government advisory body this week.
He said he hoped the investigation would reverse the popular belief that Deng ordered the crackdown.
"Deng Xiaoping was not necessarily aware of the entire situation then," Wu said. "We should clear things up."
Wu blamed the decision to open fire on unarmed demonstrators on Beijing's disgraced Communist Party boss and ex-mayor Chen Xitong, who has not been seen in public since April 1995.
"It wouldn't be too much to mete out 10 death sentences to Chen Xitong," Wu said.
Chen stepped down as the capital's party boss after his protege, vice-mayor Wang Baosen, committed suicide in April 1995 after coming under investigation for corruption.
Chen is under house arrest in northern Inner Mongolia, Hong Kong's China-watching newspapers say.
He was ousted from the Communist Party's powerful Politburo in September 1995, becoming the most senior official to be ensnared in a corruption scandal since the communists swept to power in 1949.
Officials declined to comment on Wu's proposals.
For bereaved relatives of demonstrators killed when the tanks rolled into Beijing, Deng must be found guilty -- even after his death.
Relatives of victims and critics of the government have called for a reassessment of the demonstrations.
China has justified the bloody crackdown, saying the protests were a counter-revolutionary rebellion.
Deng never showed any sign of remorse for what is regarded as the bloodiest episode of his career.

His children, who were reported to have tried to dissuade him in 1989 from using force, have hinted privately that they expect official history to review the current verdict on the massacre and add a bloody stain to their father's reputation.
Wu stopped short of calling for a reassessment of the demonstrations, but defended the students.
"The students were not rebelling," Wu said, adding that they were merely demonstrating against corruption.
Wu is best known for his 1942 play "Going Home on a Snowy and Windy Night" about the mistress of a government official having an affair with a Beijing opera star.
Student leaders of the 1989 demonstrations have either fled into exile abroad or been jailed.

Wang Dan, 26, one of the most prominent student leaders, was jailed for four years for his role in the demonstrations. He was re-imprisoned last year to serve 11 years on charges of plotting to subvert the government.
